questions.enonce_markdown:
How important was Zaid in the compilation of the Qur'an?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The Qur'an was revealed to the Prophet Muhammad over about twenty-three years, and according to Islamic tradition it was memorised and written down during his lifetime. The collection of the revelation into one book took place after his death in two stages, under Abu Bakr and under Uthman. Zaid ibn Thabit, a young man of the Ansar of Medina, had a central role in both stages, and this answer examines how important he was.

**1. Zaid's qualifications.**
- He was one of the main scribes of the revelation for the Prophet in Medina, and he had memorised the Qur'an.
- Tradition says that he was present at the final review of the Qur'an in the last year of the Prophet's life and that he knew the order of the revelation.
- He was young, intelligent, trusted and known for his honesty, and he was a keen student of languages, so he was a suitable choice for a work needing accuracy.

**2. The first collection under Abu Bakr (about 632-633).**
- After the battle of Yamama, in the wars against false prophets, many of the reciters (*qurra*) who had memorised the Qur'an were killed. Umar feared that part of the Qur'an might be lost with the death of the reciters, and urged Caliph Abu Bakr to have it collected.
- Abu Bakr asked Zaid to do it. According to the tradition, Zaid at first hesitated, finding the task too heavy, but he accepted. He searched for the Qur'an among the written pieces made of palm leaf stalks, flat stones, pieces of leather and bone and in the memory of men, and accepted a passage only when it was confirmed by writing and by witnesses who had heard it from the Prophet.
- The pages (*suhuf*) were kept by Abu Bakr, then by Umar, and then by Umar's daughter Hafsa, the widow of the Prophet.

**3. The standard copy under Uthman (about 650).**
- During the reign of Uthman, differences arose in the recitation among Muslims in the newly conquered lands. A commander, Hudhayfa, warned Uthman and asked him to act before the community fell into disagreement, as other communities had on their scriptures.
- Uthman obtained the pages from Hafsa and appointed Zaid, with other men of Quraysh (such as Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, Sa'id ibn al-As and Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith), to copy them into volumes. Where Zaid and the Qurayshi members disagreed on a word, it was to be written in the dialect of the Quraysh, in which the Qur'an was revealed.
- Copies were sent to the main centres of the Muslim world, and other versions, whether in fragments or complete, were withdrawn. The text became the standard used by Muslims to this day.

**4. Assessment of his importance.** Zaid was very important: he was the skilled scribe, the chief worker in both stages, and the careful editor whose method of checking the text by memory and writing protected its accuracy. Without his work, the collecting of the sheets and the creation of the standard copy would have been difficult. But his importance should not be exaggerated: the initiative came from Umar and Abu Bakr, the authority from the caliphs, and the text itself was preserved by the memory of many reciters and by written records made during the Prophet's lifetime. Zaid served the community and the caliphs; he did not work alone.

**Conclusion.** Zaid ibn Thabit was of very great importance in the compilation of the Qur'an as the main person who carried out both the first collection and the standard copy. His reliability and skill made him the right man for the task, and the form of the Qur'an used today is closely linked to his work.
